w: What's tested Who came up with which idea The two old schools and what they learned Today's competing ideas and what they agree on The four modern rules: back-teeth support first, a good bite plane, the right kind of contacts, and front-teeth guidance Dawson's smile-design steps and speech checks Real patients rarely look like the perfect model, but the same principles still apply. They came from about 175 years of ideas, first for dentures and later for natural teeth. History Bonwill, the "father of articulation," found that the two jaw joints and the chin make a triangle with sides about 4 inches. That led to the idea of a bite plane and to balanced dentures, where teeth touch everywhere so the denture doesn't tip. Balkwill saw the moving joint shift inward during sideways movement; von Spee described the side-view curve; Christensen saw the back teeth separate when the jaw moves forward and made a record of it; Parfitt first put curved joint paths on an articulator; Bennett described the jaw's sideways shift. Monson combined these into the idea that the teeth sit on a 4-inch ball; his articulator spun around a center point instead of copying the joints. Two schools Pankey, Mann and Schuyler built the lower back teeth to Monson's curve, then shaped the upper back teeth from paths the patient ground into wax. They didn't think an articulator needed to copy the joints. Schuyler later dropped the balancing contacts, made the front-teeth guidance more important, and used simpler tools. Gnathology tried to copy the patient exactly: find the joints' hinge centers, trace every movement, and set a fully adjustable articulator. Early on it pushed the jaw all the way back (rearmost, uppermost, midmost) and used balanced contacts, both mistakes. Gnathologists later gave us canine guidance (Stallard and Stuart; keyword: separation) and mutually protected occlusion (D'Amico; keyword: force), plus P.K. Thomas's waxing. Digital jaw tracking has brought the "copy the patient" goal back. Today's ideas Conformative: keep what the patient has (most everyday dentistry, if things are healthy). Gnathology: copy the joints' movement. Pankey/Dawson: respect the seated joint and focus on front-teeth guidance. Bioesthetics: good looks and good function go together; bite height set from a fixed measurement; strong front overlap. Neuromuscular: build the bite where muscles are most relaxed, found with an electrical stimulator; this usually means raising the bite and redoing every tooth, and it puts the jaw too far forward, so UAB doesn't teach it. All of them agree that all teeth should touch at once and back teeth shouldn't bump when the jaw moves. Speer's test for any idea: does it work for every patient, and can you do it without drilling teeth? Four rules 1. Back-tooth support comes first. Without back teeth, the front teeth take all the force and break down, and the bite collapses. Fixing only the six front teeth a patient wants won't last. You don't need every molar: teeth back to the second premolar (a "shortened dental arch") work fine. 2. Fix the bite plane. Teeth that drift or over-erupt get in the way of every movement. Small problems can be smoothed (enameloplasty), bigger ones crowned, and severe ones may need the tooth removed. 3. Use the right contacts. The old "tripod" contact (each cusp touching three spots) is very stable but hard to make, especially in porcelain, and needs the teeth to separate right away. Today we use point to flat surface: forces go straight down the root and there's a little "freedom" to slide, side to side for the jaw's sideways shift, and front to back for a small slide (a "long centric"). 4. Front-teeth guidance matters most. The back (tongue) side of the upper front teeth must fit the paths the jaw actually uses. To rebuild it: wax it up, try it in temporaries, record the paths on a custom guide table, and copy them in the final crowns. Dawson's smile design In order: set the holding contacts; check lip support (a bulge at the gumline usually means the tooth wasn't trimmed enough); make sure the lips close easily; check "f" and "v" against the lower lip and the smile line; shape the tongue side for smooth guidance; round the bump near the gum (cingulum) for "d" and "t" (too bulky can push teeth forward in a tongue-thruster); and check "s": too much space causes a lisp, too little a whistle.
